text: They named her after a river nobody could find on any map, and that was the first lie and the kindest one. She came up out of the bottomland with mud to her knees and a memory she did not own, a memory that owned her instead, walking her down to the water at night the way a hand walks a child to church. The women said hush. The women always said hush, as if quiet were a place you could put a thing and the thing would stay. But it did not stay. It rose. It rose in the cornbread and the candle wax and the small bones of the chickens; it rose in the way the men looked away from her and the way the dogs would not. Listen. There is a sorrow older than the field, older than the boat, older than the breaking, and it lives in the throat of every woman who has had to choose. She chose. She chose and she carried it and she did not set it down, not at the crossroads, not at the grave, not even at the table where they finally, finally, fed her. Hush, they said. And she opened her mouth, and out came the river, and out came the names, and out came everybody who had ever been lost.

Cinnamon. That was the smell of the house before the burning, before the men with their orderly fire and their orderly mouths. Cinnamon and lye and the particular sweetness of a porch board warmed all day by a sun that asked nothing in return. Pauline kept it so. Pauline scrubbed the world into shape every morning the way you scrub a sin, knowing it would come back, knowing the coming back was the point. Her hands were maps of everywhere she had not been allowed to go. Her hands knew the weight of a sleeping baby and the weight of a dead one and could not, would not, tell you which was heavier, because to weigh them was to choose, and she had done enough choosing. The neighbors called her proud. They meant unbroken, and they could not forgive it. So they watched and they waited and they fed the small fire of their watching until the day came, the day always comes, when a woman who will not bend becomes a woman they may burn. But she had already given the cinnamon to her daughters. She had already pressed it into their wrists. Smell, she told them. Remember this is what we were before they decided what we are. And the girls smelled, and the girls remembered, and the burning could not reach that far back.

Down in the deep of the quarter there was a tree the old folks said could hear you, and they were right, though right is a small word for it. It heard the boy who hanged a wish in its branches and the girl who buried her courage at its root and the grandmother who came every spring to argue with God under its leaves. It heard, and it kept, and it grew thick on the keeping. You could lay your hand against the bark and feel a hundred years of want pushing back. That was the thing about that ground: it did not let go. It held the placentas and the milk teeth and the names whispered into mason jars; it held the men who left and the women who stayed and the difference between leaving and being taken, which is everything, which is nothing, which is the whole of it. Sethe knew. Baby knew. Everybody who ever stood barefoot on that red dirt knew that the dead are not gone, only patient, only waiting in the long grass for somebody to call them properly, by their right names, in the right order, with the door propped open and a plate set out and the lamp turned low so they will not be afraid of how much they have been missed.

She loved him the way the drowning love air, which is to say completely, and without dignity, and far too late. He had a laugh that could undo a row of buttons from across a room, and a silence that could close a coffin, and First Corinthians had spent twenty years learning the country between the two. Love is not a feeling, her mother had told her, scrubbing a pot that was already clean. Love is a labor. Love is getting up in the dark. But the mother was wrong, or the mother was tired, or the mother had simply not been loved the way the girl was loved, badly, electrically, like a wire down in a storm. There are women who give and women who are emptied; the world has a use for both and a name for neither. So she gave. She gave until the giving was a habit and the habit was a self and she could no longer find, underneath, the green girl who had once wanted only to be wanted back. Where did she go, that girl. Where do any of them go, the ones we set down to make room for a man, a child, a country that asked everything and called it love. She is in the river. She is always in the river. And the river remembers, even when we cannot.

Sundays the town wore its grief like good shoes, tight and shining and meant to be seen. The choir let it out slow, note by salted note, and the deacons caught it in their handkerchiefs, and the children, who did not yet know what they were practicing for, learned the shape of sorrow in their small straight backs. This was the inheritance. Not the land, which was never theirs, not the gold, which was a story, but this: the knowing of how to carry a heavy thing a long way without dropping it on the road. Macon's people had carried each other up out of the swamp and across the line and into the cold cities that ate them politely, and they had not dropped one, not one, though the arms ached and the years were long and some of them had wanted, God forgive them, to set the burden down and walk free into the indifferent morning. But you do not. You do not set down your own. You shift the weight. You hum. You call the next one by name to remind yourself there is a next one. And on the far side of all that carrying, if there is a far side, the dead will be waiting with cool water and a place to sit, and they will say, at last, in the only voice that ever mattered: you brought them. You brought us all the way home.
